front: What is a proposition?
back: A declarative statement of fact with a truth value — either true or false, never both.

front: What does ¬p mean?
back: It is not the case that p. Negation has the opposite truth value to p.

front: When is p ∧ q true?
back: Both p and q must be true; false otherwise.

front: When is p ∨ q true?
back: At least one is true, including when both are true. Or is inclusive by default.

front: When is p ⊕ q true?
back: Exactly one proposition is true, not both.

front: When is p → q false?
back: Only when p is true and q is false: the condition is met but the result does not follow.

front: When is p ↔ q true?
back: When p and q have the same truth value.

front: Give the converse of p → q.
back: q → p.

front: Give the inverse of p → q.
Give the contrapositive of p → q.
back: ¬q → ¬p. This is equivalent to the original implication.

front: Which Table 7/8 identities may you cite?
back:
Only these three:
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q (7.1)
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (contrapositive)
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
All of Table 6 is allowed. Everything else must be derived.

front: State De Morgan for ¬(p ∧ q).
back: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q — negate each piece and flip the connective.

front: State De Morgan for ¬(p ∨ q).
What is a tautology?
back: A compound proposition that is always true, no matter the truth values of its individual propositions.

front: What does ∀x P(x) mean?
back: For every x in the domain, P(x) is true.

front: What does ∃x P(x) mean?
back: There exists some (at least one) x in the domain so that P(x) is true.

front: Negate ∀x P(x).
back: ∃x ¬P(x). Flip the quantifier, negate the inside.

front: Negate ∃x P(x).
Does ∀x distribute over ∨?
back: No. ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)) ≢ ∀x P(x) ∨ ∀x Q(x). Different x may satisfy different predicates.

front: Can mixed quantifiers be swapped?
back: Not in general. ∀x∃y allows y to depend on x; ∃y∀x requires one y for every x.

front: State modus ponens.
back:
p
p → q
∴ q

front: State modus tollens.
back:
¬q
p → q
∴ ¬p

front: Can a valid argument have false premises?
back: Yes. Validity says that if all premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

front: Define an even integer.
back: An integer n is even if there exists some integer k so that n = 2k.

front: Define an odd integer.
back: An integer n is odd if there exists some integer k so that n = 2k + 1.

front: Define a rational number.
back: A real number x is rational if there exist integers p, q with q ≠ 0 so that x = p/q.

front: Does ℕ include 0 in this class?
What is a set?
back: An unordered collection of distinct objects which we call elements.

front: What is P(S)?
back: The set of all subsets of S. If |S| = n, then |P(S)| = 2ⁿ.

front: Are ∅ and {∅} equal?
back: No. ∅ has 0 elements. {∅} has 1 element: the empty set.

front: Is a false declarative statement still a proposition?
back: Yes. “8 is prime” is a false proposition.

front: Negate x < 3.
Translate “p but not q.”
back: p ∧ ¬q.

front: What is the only false row of p ∨ q?
back: p = F and q = F.

front: How do you decide whether an English “or” is exclusive?
back: Default is inclusive ∨. “Either … or” is a cue to check for exclusivity (⊕); an explicit “or both” makes it inclusive.

front: How do ∨ and ⊕ differ on TT?
back: ∨ is true; ⊕ is false.

front: List the English phrasings of p → q.
back:
All of these mean p → q:
if p, then q
p only if q
q if p
q whenever p
q is necessary for p
p is sufficient for q
q unless ¬p

front: Translate “q is necessary for p.”
back: p → q.

front: Expand p ↔ q using conditionals.
Is the converse equivalent to the original?
back: Not generally; p = F, q = T separates them.

front: Which related statement is equivalent to the inverse?
back: The converse.

front: Give the contrapositive of (p ∧ q) → r.
How many rows does a truth table with n variables have, and in what order is it filled?
back: 2ⁿ rows, one per assignment. Compute inner subexpressions first, then the outer connective.

front: How many rows for p, q, r?
State the precedence of the logical operators.
back: Parentheses first; then ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ from strongest to weakest binding. Parenthesize XOR and chained implications.

front: Parse ¬p ∨ q ∧ r with default precedence.
back: (¬p) ∨ (q ∧ r). Negation binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨.

front: Define a contradiction (compound proposition).
back: A compound proposition that is always false, whatever the truth values of its variables.

front: Define a contingency.
back: A compound proposition that is true on some assignments and false on others.

front: What does p ≡ q mean, and how is it proved?
back: p ↔ q is a tautology. Prove it with matching truth-table columns or a chain of already-known equivalences.

front: How is a successive-substitution proof written?
back: One equivalent expression per line, each labeled with the law that justifies the change; end with ∎.

front: Negate p → q using only allowed laws (show each step).
back:
¬(p → q)
≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q) — 7.1
≡ ¬¬p ∧ ¬q — De Morgan
≡ p ∧ ¬q — double negation

front: How do you prove a tautology using equivalences?
back: Reduce the expression to T using only allowed laws, one substitution per line, ending “≡ T” with its law and ∎.

front: State the identity law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∧ T ≡ p
p ∨ F ≡ p

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∧ T ≡ p?
back: Identity.

front: State the domination law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ T ≡ T
p ∧ F ≡ F

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∨ T ≡ T?
back: Domination.

front: State the idempotent law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ p ≡ p
p ∧ p ≡ p

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∨ p ≡ p?
back: Idempotent.

front: State the double negation law (Table 6), both forms.
Which Table 6 law is ¬¬p ≡ p?
back: Double negation.

front: State the commutative law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p
p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p?
back: Commutative.

front: State the associative law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∨ r
p ∧ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∧ r

front: Which Table 6 law is (p ∨ q) ∨ r ≡ p ∨ (q ∨ r)?
back: Associative.

front: State the distributive law (Table 6), both forms.
Which Table 6 law is p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)?
back: Distributive.

front: Which law is ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q?
back: De Morgan.

front: State the absorption law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p
p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p?
back: Absorption.

front: State the negation law (Table 6), both forms.
back:
p ∨ ¬p ≡ T
p ∧ ¬p ≡ F

front: Which Table 6 law is p ∧ ¬p ≡ F?
back: Negation.

front: What is a propositional function?
back: A statement P(x) whose truth depends on an input x. It becomes a proposition once every input is specified or bound by a quantifier.

front: What changes a predicate into a proposition?
back: Specify all free inputs, or bind them with quantifiers over a domain.

front: What is the domain of a quantified statement?
back: The set of allowed inputs. Stipulations on the subject (“positive reals”, “students in this class”) are part of the statement’s meaning.

front: Why is ∀x (x² ≥ x) false over ℝ?
back: x = 1/2 is a counterexample: (1/2)² = 1/4 < 1/2.

front: How many counterexamples refute ∀x P(x)?
back: One element of the domain where P is false.

front: What establishes ∃x P(x)?
back: One witness x in the domain for which P(x) is true.

front: What is a counterexample to ∀x P(x)?
back: A domain element a with P(a) false. One suffices. (To refute ∃x P(x) you must show every element fails.)

front: Refute ∀x ∈ ℕ(x² > 0).
back: x = 0 is a counterexample.

front: When is a variable bound, and when is it free?
back: Bound when it lies in the scope of its matching quantifier; otherwise free. A statement with a free variable need not have a fixed truth value.

front: Which variable is free in ∀x P(x, y)?
back: y is free; x is bound.

front: Which quantifier distributions are genuine equivalences?
back:
Equivalences:
∀x (P ∧ Q) ≡ ∀x P ∧ ∀x Q
∃x (P ∨ Q) ≡ ∃x P ∨ ∃x Q
Not equivalences: ∀ over ∨, ∃ over ∧.

front: Is ∃x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ≡ ∃x P(x) ∧ ∃x Q(x)?
back: No. The two witnesses may be different elements. ∃ distributes over ∨ only.

front: Negate “Some student in this class is taking Calc 3.”
back:
No student in this class is taking Calc 3.
∀x ¬T(x), domain: students in this class.

front: Translate “All A are B” and “Some A are B.”
back: ∀x (A(x) → B(x)) and ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)). State the domain and define each predicate first.

front: Why use ∧ in “some A are B”?
back: The same witness must actually be A and B.

front: When is a quantifier nested?
back: When it lies in the scope of another quantifier. A predicate with several inputs takes one quantifier per variable.

front: What does ∀x∃y P(x, y) allow y to depend on?
back: The previously chosen x.

front: Which quantifier orders may be swapped?
back: Same kind: ∀x∀y ≡ ∀y∀x and ∃x∃y ≡ ∃y∃x. Mixed orders cannot in general; ∃y∀x P(x, y) implies ∀x∃y P(x, y) but not conversely.

front: Which is stronger: ∃y∀x P or ∀x∃y P?
back: ∃y∀x P; one common witness works for every x.

front: Over ℝ, give the truth values of the four nests for x + y = 0.
back:
∀x∀y: F
∀x∃y: T (take y = −x)
∃x∀y: F (given x, take y = 1 − x)
∃x∃y: T (0, 0)

front: Why is ∃x∀y (x+y = 0) false over ℝ?
back: For any proposed x, choose y = 1−x; then the sum is 1.

front: In what order do you translate a nested English statement?
back: Specify each variable’s domain and predicate. Universal choices come before the witnesses that may depend on them.

front: Translate: every nonzero real has a multiplicative inverse.
Write “there is exactly one x with P(x)” using quantifiers.
back:
∃x (P(x) ∧ ∀z (P(z) → z = x))
Existence, then uniqueness of the witness.

front: What two ingredients does exactly one require?
back: Existence, then uniqueness of the witness.

front: How do you negate a nested quantified statement?
back: Push ¬ inward one quantifier at a time, flipping each while keeping their order; then negate the innermost predicate or connective.

front: Negate ∀x∃y∀z P(x, y, z).
back: ∃x∀y∃z ¬P(x, y, z)

front: Does “none of a student’s friends are friends with each other” assert that the student has friends?
back: No. It is a universal statement, so it is vacuously true for a student with no friends.

front: Define an argument (logic).
back: A sequence of propositions, the premises, followed by a conclusion.

front: When is an argument form valid?
back: Whenever all premises are true, the conclusion is true. Equivalently (p₁ ∧ … ∧ pₙ) → q is a tautology.

front: How can a valid argument have a false conclusion?
back: At least one premise must be false.

front: How is a step / reason table written?
back: Each premise or derived statement is a numbered step; the reason names the rule or law and the earlier steps it uses. End with ∎.

front: How do equivalences and inference rules differ inside a derivation?
back: Equivalences go both ways; inference rules go one way. An allowed equivalence may replace a statement, citing the step it came from.

front: May you use the contrapositive as a step in a derivation?
back: Yes. It is an allowed equivalence, so cite the original step and the law.

front: How do you show an argument form is invalid?
back: Exhibit one truth assignment that makes every premise true and the conclusion false.

front: Name the two fallacies and give their forms.
back:
Affirming the conclusion: p → q, q ∴ p
Denying the hypothesis: p → q, ¬p ∴ ¬q
Both are invalid.

front: Name the fallacy: p → q, ¬p ∴ ¬q
back: Denying the hypothesis. Invalid: p = F, q = T makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

front: How do you verify that an inference rule is valid?
back: Show that (conjunction of premises) → conclusion is a tautology.

front: Which proposition must be a tautology for modus ponens to be valid?
Which rule is p; p → q ∴ q?
back: Modus ponens.

front: Which rule is ¬q; p → q ∴ ¬p?
back: Modus tollens.

front: State hypothetical syllogism.
back:
p → q
q → r
∴ p → r

front: Which rule is p → q; q → r ∴ p → r?
back: Hypothetical syllogism.

front: State disjunctive syllogism.
back:
p ∨ q
¬p
∴ q

front: Which rule is p ∨ q; ¬p ∴ q?
back: Disjunctive syllogism.

front: State addition.
back:
p
∴ p ∨ q

front: Which rule is p ∴ p ∨ q?
back: Addition.

front: State simplification.
back:
p ∧ q
∴ p

front: Which rule is p ∧ q ∴ p?
back: Simplification.

front: State conjunction.
back:
p
q
∴ p ∧ q

front: Which rule is p; q ∴ p ∧ q?
back: Conjunction.

front: State resolution.
back:
p ∨ q
¬p ∨ r
∴ q ∨ r

front: Which rule is p ∨ q; ¬p ∨ r ∴ q ∨ r?
back: Resolution.

front: How do you prove p → q directly?
back: Pf Suppose p. Use definitions and algebra to establish q. ∎
2k² + 2k. So the square of an odd integer is odd.

front: Define a perfect square.
back: An integer n is a perfect square if there exists an integer k so that n = k².

front: Why is the product of two perfect squares a perfect square?
back: k² · j² = (kj)², and kj ∈ ℤ.

front: How do you prove p → q by contraposition?
back: State C.P.: If ¬q then ¬p. Then prove that directly: suppose ¬q and derive ¬p.

front: Prove: if 3n + 2 is odd then n is odd. Which method, and how does it go?
back: Contraposition. Suppose n is even, n = 2k. Then 3n + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1) with 3k + 1 ∈ ℤ, so 3n + 2 is even. ∎

front: State the small-factor lemma for n = ab.
back: If n = ab with positive integers a, b, then a ≤ √n or b ≤ √n (inclusive or). Proved by contraposition.

front: Negate a ≤ √n or b ≤ √n.
back: a > √n and b > √n.

front: How do you prove p by contradiction?
back: Assume ¬p and derive a contradiction r ∧ ¬r. Name the contradiction explicitly at the end.

front: What form must the contradiction take at the end of the proof?
back: r ∧ ¬r for some statement r, stated explicitly (e.g. the fraction was reduced, yet both parts are even).

front: Outline the proof that √2 is irrational.
back: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Then p² = 2q², so p is even, p = 2k. Then q² = 2k², so q is even. Both even contradicts lowest terms. ∎

front: What is the contradiction in the √2 proof?
back: The fraction was reduced, but p and q are both even and share factor 2.

front: How do you prove p → q by contradiction?
back: Assume p and ¬q (the negation of the implication) and derive a contradiction.

front: Negate p → q before a contradiction proof.
back: p ∧ ¬q — the implication fails exactly when p holds and q does not.

front: Outline the proof that an irrational plus a rational is irrational.
back: Suppose x is irrational, r = a/b is rational, and x + r = c/d is rational. Then x = c/d − a/b = (cb − ad)/(bd) is rational: contradiction. ∎

front: Must a sum of two irrationals be irrational?
How do you prove p ↔ q?
back: Prove both directions, labeled (→) p → q and (←) q → p. Different methods may be used for each.

front: How do you prove several statements are equivalent (TFAE)?
back: Prove a cycle p₁ → p₂ → p₃ → p₁. Transitivity supplies every remaining direction.

front: Which three arrows suffice for a, b, c TFAE?
back: a → b, b → c, c → a.

front: Outline the proof that ∛2 is irrational.
back: Lemma (by contraposition): n³ even ⇒ n even. Then assume ∛2 = p/q reduced; p³ = 2q³ makes p even, p = 2k, so q³ = 4k³ makes q even: contradiction. ∎

front: Which lemma does the ∛2 proof need, and how is it proved?
back: n³ even ⇒ n even. Contrapose: if n = 2k + 1 then n³ = 2(4k³ + 6k² + 3k) + 1 is odd.

front: Do duplicates change a set?
back: No; its elements are distinct.

front: Name the three ways to describe a set.
back: Roster (list the elements), set-builder (state the qualifying property), and interval notation for real numbers between endpoints.

front: Which endpoints are included in (a, b]?
back: b is included; a is excluded.

front: List the standard number sets and their symbols.
Is ℕ = ℤ⁺ in this class?
back: No. 0 ∈ ℕ but 0 ∉ ℤ⁺.

front: What is a singleton?
back: A set containing exactly one element.

front: When are two sets equal?
back: A = B iff every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A; equivalently A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.

front: Does |A| = |B| imply A = B?
back: No: {1} and {2} both have one element but differ.

front: What is the universal set U?
back: The set of all objects under consideration in the current problem. It depends on context.

front: Define A ⊆ B and say how to prove it.
back: A ⊆ B means ∀x (x ∈ A → x ∈ B). To prove it, take an arbitrary x ∈ A and show x ∈ B.

front: How do you disprove A ⊆ B?
back: Find x ∈ A with x ∉ B.

front: Define a proper subset A ⊂ B.
back: A ⊆ B and A ≠ B: every element of A is in B and some element of B is not in A. Also written A ⊊ B.

front: Which two subset facts hold for every set A?
back: ∅ ⊆ A (vacuously true implication) and A ⊆ A (reflexive).

front: Why is ∅ ⊆ A always true?
back: There are no elements of ∅ that could violate the inclusion.

front: Define the cardinality of a finite set.
back: If S has exactly n distinct elements for some nonnegative integer n, S is finite and |S| = n. Otherwise S is infinite.

front: What is |{{1}}|?
back: 1. Its only element is {1}.

front: What is P({∅})?
back: {∅,{∅}}, with two elements.

front: How do ∈ and ⊆ differ for nested sets?
back: x ∈ A removes one brace level: x is an element. A ⊆ B compares elements without removing a level. {1} ∈ {{1}} but {1} ⊄ {{1}}.
No, since 1 is not an element of {{1}}.

front: Define theorem.
back: A fact that can be proven true; the main fact.

front: Define proposition (proof vocabulary).
back: A theorem of lesser prominence; a supporting detail.

front: Define axiom.
back: A statement assumed true without proof.

front: Define proof.
back: A valid argument establishing the truth of a theorem.

front: Define lemma.
back: A theorem used to prove another result.

front: Define corollary.
back: A theorem that follows directly from a theorem just proved.

front: Define conjecture.
back: A statement proposed to be true but not yet proven.

front: Translate: p is sufficient for q
back: p → q. The sufficient condition is the hypothesis.

front: Translate: q if p
back: p → q. In “q if p,” the part after “if” is the hypothesis.

front: Translate: a necessary condition for p is q
back: p → q. The necessary condition is the conclusion.

front: Translate: q unless ¬p
back: p → q. “q unless ¬p” means if p then q.

front: Translate: p only if q
back: p → q. “Only if” introduces the conclusion.

front: Give the one-line rule for choosing a proof method.
back:
Positive hypothesis → direct
Unhelpful hypothesis, conclusion easy to negate → contraposition
Bare negative claim → contradiction
If-then with a negative conclusion contraposition doesn’t fix → contradiction of an implication
“iff” → both directions
“equivalent” → cycle
“prove or disprove” → try to break it first

front: When is a direct proof the right choice?
back: The hypothesis is a positive, unpackable property (even, odd, rational, perfect square) and the conclusion is positive. You can write “there exists k so that …” immediately.

front: When should you switch to contraposition?
back:
The hypothesis is hard to unpack but the negated conclusion is easy.
Tells: conclusion “n is even/odd” with a hypothesis about 3n + 2, n³ + 5, mn or n²; an “or” conclusion; “x irrational ⇒ 1/x irrational”.

front: When is contradiction of a proposition the method?
back:
The statement is not an if-then and is a negative claim: “√2 is irrational”, “there is no rational r with …”.
Tells: irrational, no, not, there is no, roots.

front: When do you use contradiction of an implication?
back:
It is an if-then, the conclusion is negative, and contraposition would still leave an irrational or negative hypothesis to unpack.
Assume p and ¬q, derive a contradiction.
Example: x irrational, y rational ⇒ x + y irrational.

front: What does “if and only if” tell you to do?
back: Prove both directions, (→) and (←), possibly by different methods.

front: How do you handle “show these statements are equivalent”?
back: Prove a cycle p₁ → p₂ → p₃ → p₁; transitivity gives every other direction.

front: What do you do first with “prove or disprove”?
back: Test small examples (0, 1, 2, √2 pairs) to try to break it. False → counterexample. True → whichever method proves it.

front: Which method for “if 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd”, and why?
back: Contraposition. The hypothesis is about 3n + 2 and cannot be unpacked; the negated conclusion “n is even” gives n = 2k at once.

front: Which method for “if x is irrational and y is rational, then x + y is irrational”, and why?
back: Contradiction of an implication. The conclusion is negative and contraposing still leaves irrationality to unpack; assume x + y rational and get x = (x + y) − y rational.

front: Which method for “√6 is irrational”, and why?
back: Contradiction of a proposition. It is a bare negative claim, not an if-then: assume √6 = p/q in lowest terms.
